proposals.relationship: Corbin credits reading Febvre during his university training with orienting him toward historical psychology and the history of sensibilities.
proposals.evidence_note: Corbin’s own 1993 interview says Michel de Bouard recommended Febvre and that Corbin repeatedly returned to his work. De Bouard retains this mediating teaching role. This is a named formative reading, not an inference from Annales affiliation, exclusive sensory-history priority or direct personal instruction by Febvre. Only the interview’s printed p. 7 was freshly checked; Febvre’s complete books and the remaining interview pages were not read here.
primary_locators: Politix 6.21 (1993), printed p. 7, first answer: Lorsque j’étais en licence ... Michel de Bouard ... lire Lucien Febvre; the answer continues with psychology, sensibilities and his wish to follow that perspective.

proposals.relationship: Corbin explains his departure from Labrousse’s economic-to-mentalities model when subsistence practices and unreliable statistics frustrated his study of the Limousin.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview given in 2003, read in Christian Pierre Kasper’s 2005 Portuguese translation, pp. 14–15. Corbin describes abandoning much of the model, not every quantitative method or all of Labrousse’s work. Bertrand Gille, whom Labrousse recommended, was his actual supervisor and helped prompt the methodological change; Labrousse is not silently substituted for Gille.
primary_locators: Revista Brasileira de História 25.49 (2005), printed pp. 14–15: Labrousse’s referral to Gille, account of the economic/social/mentalities sequence, difficulties quantifying subsistence and Gille’s warning about statistics. Interview date 21 November 2003 recorded on p. 12.

proposals.relationship: Corbin reports Prost’s criticism that his historical practice gives insufficient attention to history’s civic and social mission.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly Corbin’s own recollection in the 2006 Vacarme interview, not a newly located text by Prost. Corbin acknowledges that the description may be right and explains his resistance to lessons-of-history arguments. His later 2013 interview also recalls Prost’s contrast between civic mission and writing for pleasure. This is a specific disagreement between colleagues, not generalized hostility or rejection of the quality of Corbin’s research.
primary_locators: Vacarme, question On ne vous connaît d’ailleurs pas pour vos prises de position ...; answer begins Antoine Prost, avec qui j’ai longtemps travaillé, me l’a reproché (opening third of interview).
Existing 2013 La Vie des idées transcript: answer beginning Oui, je ne crois pas qu’on puisse vraiment écrire l’histoire sans plaisir.

proposals.relationship: Corbin uses Foucault’s analysis of medical attention to sexuality and sexual classification to frame his own questions about bodily practices before the later nineteenth century.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2003 interview read in the credited 2005 translation, pp. 29–30. He praises La Volonté de savoir and explicitly invokes Foucault’s argument, while distinguishing his interest in the period before the post-1860 taxonomy of perversions. This is specified use and development, not wholesale Foucauldian affiliation or a claim that Foucault’s text directly records sexual acts. Foucault’s original book was not freshly read.
primary_locators: Printed pp. 29–30, final substantive answers: La volonté de savoir, clinical questioning about sex, and Foucault’s identification of the later science of sex.

proposals.relationship: Corbin explicitly rejects the irreversible civilizing trajectory he associates with Elias, emphasizing divergent temporalities and the contingency of historical change.
proposals.evidence_note: Corbin’s own characterization in a 2006 answer about rethinking nineteenth-century political history. The relationship records his particular objection; it does not adopt his description as a complete account of Elias’s argument. Elias’s original works were not freshly checked, and no reply by Elias is asserted.
primary_locators: Question Dans un ouvrage collectif récent, vos élèves soulignent ...; answer begins J’ai toujours refusé l’idée que l’histoire suive un cours univoque et repérable and explicitly names Norbert Elias.

proposals.relationship: Corbin criticizes the republic-centered account he associates with Furet for reducing much of nineteenth-century France to steps toward a later republican outcome.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2006 answer also names Maurice Agulhon, whose credit is retained here without inventing a standalone endpoint. Corbin argues for studying monarchies, conflicting political emotions and other periods on their own terms. This records his specific historiographical criticism, not a claim that all of Furet’s work is teleological; Furet’s original books remain unread in this dossier.
primary_locators: Same political-history answer, immediately after Elias: C’était le cas chez Maurice Agulhon, mais aussi chez François Furet; ensuing explanation of the nineteenth century pictured as waiting for the Republic and the neglected monarchies.

proposals.relationship: Corbin identifies a limit of the material anthropology associated with Braudel: reconstructing objects and environments does not by itself recover an individual’s inner life.
proposals.evidence_note: A narrow methodological objection in Corbin’s 2006 answer about accessing people who left few traces. He acknowledges how much tools and material objects can reveal. The criticism does not deny the value of material history, assert that Braudel attempted a particular biography, or imply that Corbin recovered Pinagot’s own feelings. No complete Braudel work was freshly read.
primary_locators: Question Quels sont les modes d’accès possibles ...; first answer paragraph beginning Il y a bien sûr ce qu’on appelle l’anthropologie matérielle and explicitly naming Braudel.

proposals.relationship: Corbin invokes a discussion with Le Goff about the limits of knowing historical individuals when explaining why reconstructing Pinagot’s world cannot recover his private feelings.
proposals.evidence_note: Corbin recalls Le Goff’s observation that very few medieval lives allow close personal knowledge, and uses it to distinguish a surrounding historical world from intimacy. Interview given in 2003, read in Kasper’s 2005 translation, p. 24. This is Corbin’s reported use of a methodological discussion, not Le Goff’s endorsement of Pinagot, formal supervision or a claim to read Le Goff’s original biographies. The meeting is not assigned an invented date.
primary_locators: Printed p. 24, paragraph beginning Lembro que eu participava de uma reunião com Jacques Le Goff; read with preceding statement that Pinagot’s emotions remain unknown and ensuing reconstruction of his surroundings.
